figures.caption: Figure 5: Without modifying the attention mask, the bias factor β is used to control the Positional Encodings (PEs) of learnable tokens. Subfigures (a) to (d) correspond to the changes in the PEs of learnable tokens when β from {0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00}.

Figure 1: Comparison between existing methods and SeCo. (a) Performance Instability. Learnable token insertion method, such as ICAE [17], exhibit pronounced sensitivity to the position bias factor β, which controls the positional encoding of learnable tokens (as detailed in Figure 5). Consequently, F1 scores fluctuate substantially across various benchmarks under different β configurations. (b) Semantic Fragmentation. Token A1 in Group A is semantically highly correlated with tokens B1 and B2 in Group B. However, position-based grouping rigidly partitions these semantically related tokens (highlighted in red boxes) into separate compression groups. (c) Semantic Consistency Compression (SeCo). SeCo selects the top-k tokens most relevant to the query as semantic centers. Subsequently, remaining tokens are dynamically assigned and merged directly in the semantic space based on query-centric semantic consistency.
Figure 4: Additional results on long context and summarization benchmarks compared with taskaware methods (i.e., COMI and RAM) using Qwen3-4B-Instruct as the backbone.

Table 3: Latency evaluation (in milliseconds) under a 16× compression constraint across different datasets. Compression latency and generation latency denote the latency for the compression and generation phases, respectively. Total latency is the sum of both phases. The best results are highlighted in bold, and the second-best results are underlined.

Figure 2: The Training Paradigm of SeCo. SeCo is based on an encoder-decoder architecture. The original context Xcontext and query Xquery are first encoded into hidden states, which are then compressed via a compression process (see Figure 3). During training, the encoder and decoder are fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [19].

Figure 3: The Compression Process of SeCo. Specifically, it sequentially performs four steps: I. Average Pooling Query Tokens. Obtain a single query representation q̄ via average pooling; II. Semantic Center Selection. The top-k tokens are selected as semantic center tokens based on the cosine similarity between each context token and q̄; III. Semantic Assignment. hcen. represents the selected semantic centers while hnon denotes the remaining tokens. Each non-center token is assigned to the most relevant semantic center based on v (defined in Eq. 7), where v is the product of its cosine similarity with the semantic center and q̄; IV. Consistency Merging. Each compression group is merged into a compressed representation based on the weights (defined in Eq. 8) of the tokens within the group. Specifically, the weight of the semantic center is its cosine similarity with q̄, and the weight of the non-center token is the product of their cosine similarity with q̄ and the center of their respective group.
Figure 6: Exact Match (EM) across both in-domain and out-of-domain QA datasets at different compression rates {2, 4, 8, 16, 32}.
Table 4: Ablation study on diverse benchmarks under 16× compression constraint. We use LLaMA-3.2-1B-Instruct as the backbone. ID and OOD refer to in-domain and out-of-domain datasets, respectively.
